about: Original sample interview answers for checking the AI marker. 'band' is the score range (0-10 per answer) a sensible marker should give. 'mustNot' lists things the feedback must never do. Written for DA Prep; not taken from any employer or candidate.

contexts.gs-markets: Goldman Sachs FICC and Equities Degree Apprenticeship, London. Four years, BSc Applied Finance at Queen Mary University of London. You will support traders and salespeople in fixed income, currencies, commodities and equities. We look for partnership, client service, integrity and excellence.
contexts.jpm-ops: J.P. Morgan Financial Services Degree Apprenticeship (Operations), Bournemouth. You will help make sure client trades and payments settle accurately and on time, investigate breaks and improve processes. Requirements: BBB at A level including a STEM subject.
contexts.ms-tech: Morgan Stanley Technology Professional Degree Apprenticeship, London. Four years. Rotate across technology teams building and supporting software for the firm's businesses. A levels AAB-ABB including Maths or Computer Science.
contexts.bofa-gm: Bank of America Global Markets Apprenticeship, London. Level 6 Financial Services Professional with a degree in Applied Finance. Support sales and trading desks. Values: deliver together, act responsibly, realise the power of our people, trust the team.
contexts.hsbc-cb: HSBC UK Degree Apprenticeship, Commercial Banking, Manchester. BSc Applied Retail and Commercial Banking, University of Exeter. Support relationship managers who look after business customers.

cases.question: Why Goldman Sachs, and why FICC and Equities rather than another division?
cases.answer: I first got interested in markets when I ran a mock portfolio for our school's economics society and saw how the pound moved after Bank of England decisions. FICC and Equities appeals to me because it sits closest to that: pricing risk for clients in real time. I want Goldman specifically because the apprenticeship puts you on the desk from the first year rather than in a support role, and because your business principles start with clients' interests coming first, which matched what I learned running the portfolio: the job is solving someone else's problem, not just making a trade. Speaking to a current apprentice at a Pathway CTM event, she said the hardest part was learning to communicate quickly and clearly with traders, which is something I've been practising as captain of my debating team.

cases.question: Why Goldman Sachs, and why FICC and Equities rather than another division?
cases.answer: Goldman Sachs is one of the most famous banks in the world and I want to work for the best. I like maths and I think markets are exciting because things change every day. FICC and Equities sounds like a fast-paced team where I could learn a lot.

cases.question: Why Goldman Sachs, and why FICC and Equities rather than another division?
cases.answer: Because it pays well.

cases.question: Tell me about a time you worked in a team and something went wrong. What did you do?
cases.answer: Last year four of us entered the Bank of England's Target 2.0 challenge. Two days before the deadline our forecast spreadsheet had an error that doubled our inflation figure, and the team started arguing about whose fault it was. I suggested we stop and split the problem: I rebuilt the inflation section from the source data while the others checked each remaining tab. I found the error came from a wrong cell reference, fixed it and added a check total so it couldn't happen again. We submitted on time and reached the regional final. I learned that in a crisis it's more useful to find the cause than the culprit.

cases.question: Tell me about a time you worked in a team and something went wrong. What did you do?
cases.answer: In a group project in Year 12 one person didn't do their part. We had to cover for them, which was annoying, but we still finished the presentation and got a good grade.

cases.question: If the Bank of England unexpectedly raised interest rates, what might happen to the pound and to UK government bond prices?
cases.answer: A surprise rise usually makes the pound stronger, because higher rates make holding sterling more attractive to investors. Bond prices tend to fall, because existing bonds pay a lower fixed coupon than new ones, so their price drops until the yield matches the new rates. The size of the move would depend on whether markets expect more rises to follow.

cases.question: If the Bank of England unexpectedly raised interest rates, what might happen to the pound and to UK government bond prices?
cases.answer: I think the pound would get weaker because borrowing costs more, and bond prices would go up because they pay more interest now.

cases.question: Why do you want a degree apprenticeship rather than going to university full time?
cases.answer: I learn best when I can apply things straight away. When I worked Saturdays at a supermarket I volunteered to help reconcile the tills at closing and found I enjoyed tracking down why numbers didn't match, which is basically what operations does with trades. An apprenticeship lets me get a degree while doing that for real, with a team who'll correct me as I go. I did think about university: my sister went, and I saw that she only got real experience in the summers. I'd rather build that experience every week and finish without debt, but I know it means managing study after work, so I've already been practising by doing my EPQ alongside my job.

cases.question: Why do you want a degree apprenticeship rather than going to university full time?
cases.answer: I don't want student debt and I think getting work experience is more valuable. I also want to start earning money sooner.

cases.question: Tell me about a time you had to be very accurate with detail.
cases.answer: As treasurer of our school's charity committee I kept the record of every donation from our sponsored walk, about 140 entries. When I compared my total with the bank deposit it was £35 short. Instead of assuming a counting mistake I went line by line and found two entries typed twice and one cheque that hadn't cleared. I corrected the record, chased the cheque with the sponsor and started a simple rule: every entry gets a reference number matching the paying-in slip. Since then our totals have matched every time.

cases.question: Tell me about a time you had to be very accurate with detail.

cases.question: Tell me about something technical you have built or learned on your own.
cases.answer: I built a small Python program that tracks my revision. It reads a timetable file, sends me a reminder and logs how long I studied each subject. The first version crashed whenever the file had a blank line, so I learned about exception handling and wrote tests for the edge cases I found. I then shared it with three friends and added a weekly chart because they asked for it. It taught me that the hard part of software isn't the first version but handling real users and messy data, which is what I'd expect at Morgan Stanley's scale.

cases.question: Tell me about something technical you have built or learned on your own.

cases.question: Tell me about a time you did the right thing when it would have been easier not to.
cases.answer: At my part-time job at a café, a regular customer was accidentally given £20 too much change while my supervisor was on break. It would have been easy to ignore it as the till would balance anyway once the next shift miscounted. I caught up with the customer outside, explained the mistake and he returned it. I then told my supervisor so she could note it. Afterwards she asked me to help train new staff on cash handling. For me acting responsibly means being honest even when nobody would notice, which is why Bank of America's 'act responsibly' value stood out to me.

cases.question: Tell me about a time you gave excellent service to a customer.
cases.answer: Working at a garden centre, a customer wanted a plant we'd sold out of for her daughter's wedding that weekend. Rather than just say no, I checked our other two branches' stock online, found one, and arranged for it to come over on the delivery van that afternoon. I phoned her when it arrived. She later left a review naming me, and my manager used it as an example in a team meeting. It taught me that good service means understanding why someone needs something, which is what I imagine relationship managers do for business customers.

cases.question: Tell me about a time you gave excellent service to a customer.
cases.answer: I work in a shop and I always try to be friendly and helpful to customers. Once someone couldn't find something so I showed them where it was.

cases.question: Describe a time you had several deadlines at once. How did you manage them?
cases.answer: In January of Year 13 I had three mock exams, my EPQ draft and a Duke of Edinburgh expedition plan due in the same fortnight. I listed every task with its deadline and how long I thought it would take, then blocked my evenings: maths revision first because it was the earliest exam, then EPQ writing in shorter sessions. I told my EPQ supervisor in advance that the draft might be two days late and agreed a new date rather than rushing it. I hit every other deadline and got an A in the maths mock. I now plan any busy period on a calendar first.

cases.question: Describe a time you had several deadlines at once. How did you manage them?
cases.answer: I just did them all. I work well under pressure.
